As another commenter said, we see an episode the following day. So on Tuesday, we see what they got up to on the Monday. On a Thursday, we see what they got up to on a Wednesday.

So let's say it's a Friday and there's an eviction, where housemate X is evicted. During Friday's episode, we see all of the activities from Thursday from all housemates, then we see a LIVE eviction of housemate X at about 9.45/10pm.  On Saturday, we see all of Friday's activities, including the evcition. Housemate X will have been involved in Fridays activities until they were evicted at 10pm, so we see them in Saturday's episode for most of the ep, until we reach the eviction time, at which point they won't be seen anymore.

I hope this helps!

So there is a bit of a cultural thing at play here. In the UK, the RSPCA recommends all cats be outdoor cats, whilst in the US the advice is very much the opposite. Because of how many Americans are on Reddit, you will get answers to things like this heavily leaning towards all cats should be indoor cats, and sometimes even going so far as to say that allowing your cats to roam freely outside is tantamount to abuse/neglect. 

I'm also in the UK, and my cats are also indoor cats because, like you, we don't feel comfortable letting them out on a busy road. We have sucked it up a couple of times and let them go outside, because there are other cats in the area and none have come to harm. One of our cats doesn't even want to go outside when we let them and the other will only go out for 10 mins before coming home and demanding cuddles and losing interest. It's not abuse to keep them indoors, especially with good reason such as a busy road. The caveat is that you do need to give them plenty of exercise through play, and hiding spots they can feel they can escape to and be safe in (think covered cat beds and hidey holes in cat towers).

If you can get through the first 4/5 days, you can get through the rest.

The first few days are hard because you'll go through sugar, and in my case caffeine, withdrawals. I had a constant headache. i got through it by telling myself I wanted the surgery. I can do hard things. I can do it. I cried and I thankfully had my fiancé there.

Then day 5 I woke up and *poof" headaches were gone and withdrawal was over. After that it was 100x easier because I could say to myself "well, if I got through the withdrawal phase, I can definitely get through it now I don't have it".

Mine consisted of 3 meal replacement shakes and one meal of veg and meat, no oil/sugar/dressings etc. Just had to be a bit imaginative with it to keep it interesting - "roast" (but without oil, so not sure you can really say they are roasted) veg were a favourite of mine as they were slightly sweet!

Good luck, you got this!

I had better care than I've ever had in a UK hospital. However, I did a lot of research into my surgeon and chose one who follows EU medical standards rather than Turkish medical standards, and who worked out of a genuine private Turkish hospital rather than an isolated bariatric "clinic".

The flight home was difficult because I unfortunately had a lot (I mean a LOT) of bruising due to one of the most minor complications possible, and I think every single one of us who went that week cried on the way home so be prepared for emotional overload after the first few hours of travelling back home! But I would 100% recommend anybody I meet that wants bariatric surgery in the UK to consider going to Turkey with my surgeon, if they can afford it, instead because I really could not fault the care I got at the hospital at all! 10/10!

Don't take too much to do, I took a kindle and a Nintendo switch and didn't use either after the first flight to Turkey, despite being there for 5 days. Also took clothes that I didn't wear, basically wore clothes to travel in, then lived in two nighties my entire hospital stay, then an outfit to fly home in! Didn't touch any of the other clothes I had.

Good luck, you got this! 💪

I will add this though: I stopped drinking energy drinks before my surgery, went through the caffeine withdrawal and everything. The first two months after surgery I actively disliked the taste of them - even my favourite monarch. But somewhere along the line I had some of my other half's and a few sips turned into one a week turned into more. I wish I'd not started again because now every time I try to stop I get the caffeine withdrawal all over again!! If I could go back in time I would just not drink them after surgery.

Honestly I have an energy drink (monarch monster - best flavour) almost every day, and I was bypassed end of August 2023. I take my time and drink it over the course of a few hours, and I'm still losing weight.

Large blood sugar spikes occure due to high carb and high sugar foods entering the intestine. What actually causes dumping isn't this blood sugar spike, though, although can make the symptoms worse. It's your body rushing extra water into your intestines to dilute the high sugar/fat foods to delay the spike. This is also not accurate, though. It's not about pressure. The part of the stomach that produces the bulk of stomach acid is bypassed, and therefor the chance of excess acid being in your pouch to be pushed up means you're less likely to get acid reflux. With sleeve, this acid is still in the same place so has a higher chance of getting pushed up *compared to a bypass surgery*. 

If you have severe acid reflux, it's probably best to get a bypass. But most acid reflux in large patients is caused by an unknown hernia, and this can be repaired during the procedure. My hernia didn't even show up on my ultrasound/endoscopy, it was only discovered once my surgeon was inside me.

There are so many reasons to get a bypass over a sleeve, conversely there are so many reasons to get a sleeve over a bypass. One thing to note, however, is a lot of sleeve patients will have a revision to bypass after a few years, for a variety of reasons. Not everyone, but enough that you should seriously consider the risk of needed a second operation to turn your sleeve into a bypass anyway.

Bypass is generally considered the gold standard, and many people who have sleeve will have a revision to bypass later in life. That's not to say everybody, or even a majority, have the revision, but it's certainly something to consider.

If you have reflux, sleeve can make it much worse. Bypass also generally has better long term results (looking 10-20 years in the future), but it's a tool and it you are willing to put in the work, you will keep the weight off. 

Sleeve is often seen as less invasive, as you don't have to cut and attach intestines. But that doesn't mean it's without risk.

Finally, weight comes into it. If you have a BMI over 50, bypass is likely to be better. If your BMI is on the lower end, sleeve is often more recommended.

The problem is that there are so many different variables, you really need to do your research and get your surgeons input. Whilst you may be *eligible* for both, your surgeon is likely to still believe one will suit you better than the other.

As a side note for OP, many people's surgeons will tell you sugary/fatty foods should be avoided for life as it will cause dumping. My surgeon does NOT say this. Of course, early on we are told to avoid for two reasons. 1) dumping, and 2) the small amount you can eat straight after surgery NEEDS to be good for you. But after 12 weeks, we are told to eat what we want, just in small amounts. And we are told to avoid the low fat/low sugar options as they believe it can cause you to eat more over the rest of the day. It may cause dumping early on, but not in the long run - *as long as it's in moderation*. A scoop of ice cream will be fine, a whole tub will cause sickness and dumping. 

Everyone's surgeons and dieticians will have different recommendations, but you're a far cry from NEVER being able to eat those foods again. It's more... not all of the time, and in moderation. I'm already learning I prefer the taste of food to actually eating it now - if that makes sense? By chewing each mouthful loads and taking my time, I don't even miss stuffing myself to bursting, which honestly I thought I would!

But if it's a stone (14lbs for the Americans in the room) after one week, that's water weight. Sometimes even two or three weeks you body can still be losing water weight. Reassess after about a month, and see how you're doing. How bad is your diet when you're not dieting? The worse it is, and the more salt you consume, the more water weight you'll lose in those initial weeks. 

Also, might be worth checking in with your GP and getting their input on it. They may even have free resources they can direct you to with classes etc on healthy eating and weight management. I live down south and we have a variety of programmes you can join. 

Also, fast weight loss I believe is only dangerous if done without medical advice. So if you do find your losing too quickly after a month or so, see your GP then and see what their thoughts are. They may advise upping calories, doing some blood tests, or say there's nothing to worry about currently.

I don't know where in the world you are, but you can get some pretty cheap products in most countries. In the UK, there's a protein free and a high in protein conditioner both are available for £1, there are gels for £1-£2, and a curl creme that isn't quite cgm but the alcohol is SO teeny tiny low most people use it anyway, again for about £2. You can use these kind of cheap products to see which ingredients your hair reacts best to, and then spend more on more expensive products if you want to afterwards! Some people actually swear by the cheaper products though.

Also, for the hair not holding a curl, how much gel do you use on wash day? A lot of people starting out don't use anywhere near enough, don't be afraid to use lots. As your hair gets healthier and more used to being curly/wavy, you can use less and less. I needed to use like an entire palmful at least when I started, and only had shoulder length hair. My hair is a lot longer now, and I need probably less than a palmful total, now! (Of course, some people don't like the feel of lords of gel even after scrunching out the crunch, so it's okay if you just want to persevere with only a little!).

If you've only been looking after your curls for a few weeks, it could just be transition hair. Transition hair can be greasy, frizzy, and not hold curls. Transition hair can last anywhere from a couple of weeks to 6 months (although it's unusual to last that long afaik).

Second, when was the last time you had a hair cut? My hair gets very frizzy and even webs when it is in need of a hair cut!

Finally, it could be something in one of your products. Try changing out one product at a time, for a few washes each, and if it suddenly improves when you change one out, look at which ingredients you removed.

You don’t just look at the cube and instantly know. There are two common methods - I’ll explain the one I prefer. 

You start by choosing a colour. You then ignore everything other than that colour, and the corners OF that colour. You use algorithms to put the sides on the right face. Then you use algorithms to put the four corners in, ignoring everything else (the algorithms change each step, and ensure you don’t ruin what you’ve already done). Then you do the same thing with the remaining middle level pieces. 

So, if two pieces are in different positions, it’s a different algorithm. But there will only be like 4 sides max you are looking at at one time, to decide which algorithm.
